title: Basics
intro: Nine small ideas that every arithmetic topic leans on. Each takes a few minutes.
If you already know one, answer its two quick questions and move on. If a lesson later feels hard, it will point you back to the idea it needs.

lessons.title: Now, ago and hence
lessons.plain: The words a question uses to move people forward and backward in time.
teach: Every age question talks about three kinds of moments:
- **Present** or **now**: today.
- **Ago** or **before**: in the past. "5 years ago" means take 5 away from today's age.
- **Hence** or **after**: in the future. "5 years hence" means add 5 to today's age.
"Hence" is an old word that exam papers still love. Whenever you see it, read it as "from now".
One more thing to notice early: when two moments are on opposite sides of today, the years between them **add up**. From "4 years ago" to "8 years hence" is 4 + 8 = 12 years.

example.q: Riya is 20 years old now. How old was she 6 years ago, and how old will she be 6 years hence?

checks.q: Arun is 31 now. What will his age be 9 years hence?
checks.why: Hence means from now, so add: 31 + 9 = 40.

checks.q: How many years are there between "3 years ago" and "7 years hence"?
checks.why: The two moments are on opposite sides of today, so the gaps add: 3 + 7 = 10.

lessons.title: What a ratio really says
lessons.plain: A ratio counts equal parts. Find the size of one part and everything else follows.
teach: "The ages of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 5" does **not** say A is 3 and B is 5.
It says: cut both ages into equal **parts**. A has 3 of those parts and B has 5. We do not yet know how big one part is.
So the whole job is to find **the size of one part**. You need one real number to do that, and you match it to the right number of parts:
| The question gives you | Match it to | Example with 3 : 5 |
| The sum of the two | parts added | sum 64 is 3 + 5 = 8 parts |
| The difference of the two | parts subtracted | difference 12 is 5 - 3 = 2 parts |
| One person's actual value | that person's parts | B is 40, and B has 5 parts |
Then divide: real number / matching parts = one part.
In these lessons "one part" and "1 unit" mean the same thing.

example.q: A and B are in the ratio 3 : 5 and together they add up to 64. Find B.
steps: The real number is a sum, so match it to parts added: 3 + 5 = 8 parts.
B has 5 parts, so B = 5 x 8 = 40.
Quick check: A = 3 x 8 = 24, and 24 + 40 = 64. It fits.

checks.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 2 : 7 and their sum is 45. What is one part?
checks.why: A sum matches parts added: 2 + 7 = 9 parts. One part = 45 / 9 = 5.

checks.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 7 and the bigger one is 18 more than the smaller. What is the bigger number?
checks.why: A difference matches parts subtracted: 7 - 4 = 3 parts = 18, so one part = 6. The bigger number is 7 x 6 = 42.

lessons.title: Joining two ratios
lessons.plain: When one name appears in two ratios, make that name the same number in both.
teach: Sometimes you get two ratios that share a name: A : B = 4 : 5 and B : C = 3 : 4.
B is 5 parts in the first and 3 parts in the second. Those are different-sized parts, so the two ratios cannot be read together yet.
Fix it by making B the **same number** in both. A number that both 5 and 3 go into is 15.
- Multiply the first ratio by 3: 4 : 5 becomes 12 : 15.
- Multiply the second ratio by 5: 3 : 4 becomes 15 : 20.
Now B is 15 in both, and you can write one line: A : B : C = 12 : 15 : 20.
Multiplying every number of a ratio by the same thing never changes the ratio. 4 : 5 and 12 : 15 are the same statement.

example.q: A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5. Write A : B : C.
steps: B is 3 in one ratio and 4 in the other. Both go into 12.
B is now 12 in both, so join them.

checks.q: A : B = 1 : 2 and B : C = 3 : 4. What is A : B : C?
checks.why: B is 2 and 3, so use 6. First ratio x 3 gives 3 : 6. Second ratio x 2 gives 6 : 8. Together: 3 : 6 : 8.
Divide both numbers of 6 : 10 by 2 and you get 3 : 5. Multiplying or dividing both sides by the same number keeps the ratio.

lessons.title: A number that several numbers go into
lessons.plain: Finding one convenient number that 10, 12 and 15 all divide exactly. Its formal name is the LCM.
teach: Many questions become easy if you can find **one number that several given numbers all go into exactly**. For 10 and 15, the number 30 works: 30 / 10 = 3 and 30 / 15 = 2, with nothing left over.
The smallest such number is called the **LCM** (lowest common multiple). You do not need a formal method for it. This simple routine is enough:
1. Take the **biggest** of the numbers.
2. Go through its multiples: once, twice, three times it.
3. Stop at the first one that all the other numbers go into.
For 10, 12 and 15: the biggest is 15. Try 15 (10 does not go in), 30 (12 does not), 45 (no), 60. Yes: 60 / 10 = 6, 60 / 12 = 5, 60 / 15 = 4. So 60 is the number.
If you cannot spot the smallest one quickly, any common multiple will do the job. For 10 and 15, using 150 instead of 30 gives the same final answer; the numbers along the way are just bigger.

example.q: Find a number that 12 and 18 both go into exactly.
steps: Take the bigger number, 18, and go through its multiples.
36: does 12 go into it? Yes, 3 times.

checks.q: What is the smallest number that 6 and 8 both go into exactly?
checks.why: Multiples of 8: 8 (6 does not go in), 16 (no), 24 (yes, 4 times). 48 also works but is not the smallest.

checks.q: What is the smallest number that 10, 15 and 20 all go into exactly?

lessons.title: Average means total
lessons.plain: The moment you see an average, turn it into a total. Totals are easy to work with.
teach: The average of a group is the total shared out equally: average = total / number of people.
Turn that around and you get the only form you will ever need:
**total = average x number of people**
Make this a habit. When a question says "the average age of A, B and C is 30", write "total = 90" straight away and forget the 30. Averages are awkward to move around; totals simply add and subtract.
One more rule about totals and time. Each person grows 1 year per year, so a group's total grows by **people x years**. Three people, 5 years later: the total is 15 more, not 5 more.

example.q: The average age of A, B and C is 30 years. A is 25 and B is 28. Find C.

checks.q: The average age of 4 friends is 22. What is the total of their ages?
Three sisters have a total age of 60 today. What will their total age be 4 years hence?
checks.why: Each of the three grows 4 years, so the total grows 3 x 4 = 12. 60 + 12 = 72.

lessons.title: A percent of a number
lessons.plain: Finding 24% of 5,000 without a calculator, by going through 1% and 10%.
teach: "Percent" means "out of a hundred". 24% of something is 24 of its hundredths.
The easiest way to find any percent is to find **1%** first. 1% of a number is the number divided by 100: move the decimal point two places left. 1% of 5,000 is 50.
Then multiply. 24% of 5,000 = 24 x 50 = 1,200.
For bigger percents, **10%** is a handy stepping stone (divide by 10). 30% of 1,600 is 3 lots of 160 = 480.
You will also use this backwards all the time: if you know that 36% of a sum is 1,440, then 1% is 1,440 / 36 = 40, and the whole sum, which is 100%, is 4,000.
That backwards step, "find 1%, then multiply by 100", is the most useful single move in arithmetic for this exam.

example.q: 15% of a number is 90. What is the number?
steps: Check: 10% of 600 is 60 and 5% is 30. Together 90.

checks.q: 20% of a sum is Rs 800. What is the sum?

lessons.title: Percents that are simple fractions
lessons.plain: 25% is a quarter, 20% is a fifth. Knowing a few of these makes awkward percents easy.
teach: Some percents are just familiar fractions wearing a different coat. 50% is a half. 25% is a quarter. When you recognise them, you can divide instead of multiplying, which is quicker and safer.
"25% of 480" is a quarter of 480: 120. No need to go through 1%.

This matters most for the percents that look ugly as decimals. Exam papers write 16.66% or 16 2/3% when they mean **one sixth**, and 33.33% or 33 1/3% when they mean **one third**. Treat them as the fraction and they become easy.
Here are the ones worth knowing. Read through them now; they will settle in as you meet them in questions.
| Percent | Fraction |
A percent above 100 works the same way: 125% is 100% + 25%, which is one and a quarter, or 5/4.

checks.q: 66 2/3% of a number is 160. What is the number?
checks.why: 66 2/3% is two thirds. If two thirds is 160, one third is 80, and the whole is 240.

lessons.title: Percent and fraction words
lessons.plain: How to turn "25% more than" or "two-thirds of" into a simple ratio.
teach: Questions often compare two people with a percent instead of a ratio. You can always turn it into a ratio, and then it is an ordinary ratio question.
The method: call the person you are comparing **with** 100. Then write the other person next to it.

The one trap worth learning now: **"more than" adds to the 100, "of" does not.** "200% more than B" is 300 against 100, which is 3 : 1. "200% of B" is 200 against 100, which is 2 : 1. Read that small word carefully.
Fractions work the same way. "A is 2/3 of B" means A : B = 2 : 3.
You do not need to memorise the table below. It is here so you can look things up until they stick.
| The words say A is ... B | A : B |
| 20% more than | 6 : 5 |
| 25% more than | 5 : 4 |
| 40% more than | 7 : 5 |
| 50% more than | 3 : 2 |
| 75% more than | 7 : 4 |
| 100% more than, or twice | 2 : 1 |
| 150% more than | 5 : 2 |
| 200% more than | 3 : 1 |
| 20% less than | 4 : 5 |
| 25% less than | 3 : 4 |

example.q: A's age is 40% more than B's age. Write A : B.

checks.q: "P is 50% more than Q." What is P : Q?
"P is 200% more than Q." How many times Q is P?
checks.why: "More than" adds to the 100: Q is 100, P is 100 + 200 = 300. That is 3 times.

lessons.title: Let the options help you
lessons.plain: Every question comes with five answers. Use them to check your work, and sometimes to find it.
teach: In this exam you never have to produce an answer from nothing. One of the five options is right, and that is useful in two ways.
**1. Check before you move on.** Put your answer back into the question. If every sentence of the question is still true, you are done. This takes a few seconds and catches most slips.

**2. Test options when you are stuck.** Ages come out as whole numbers. If a person has 8 parts of a ratio, that person's age must be a multiple of 8. Options that are not can be crossed out without solving anything.

And always read the **last line** again before you mark. The question may ask for the age 5 years ago, or for the sum, when you have just found today's age of one person. The option for today's age is usually sitting there waiting.

example.q: The ages of M and T are in the ratio 5 : 8. T's age five years ago was one of: 30, 35, 40, 45. Which can it be?
steps: T has 8 parts today, so T's age today is a multiple of 8.
Add 5 to each option to get today's age: 35, 40, 45, 50.

checks.q: You solved a question and found B = 42 today. The question asks for "B's age 4 years ago". What do you mark?
checks.why: The last line asks for 4 years ago: 42 - 4 = 38. Marking 42 is the most common slip in this topic.

checks.q: A's age is 7 parts of a ratio. Which of these can be A's age?
checks.why: A's age must be a multiple of 7. Only 42 = 7 x 6 is.
